urgency.h: The Driver Had Insurance. You Had a Crosswalk. Guess Who They'll Blame.
urgency.sub: Pedestrian and cyclist injuries are among the most severe on the road — and insurers fight them the hardest. Here's what they're doing right now.

cards.p: Every pedestrian case starts with the driver claiming you darted out, were on your phone, or weren't in the crosswalk. Footage, witnesses, and reconstruction settle that argument — if someone preserves them fast.

cards.t: Hit-and-run? You may still have a claim
cards.p: Your own uninsured-motorist coverage, a household policy, or the city itself may be liable. Don't assume no driver means no case.
Bad crosswalk design, a missing signal, a bus, a city vehicle — if a government entity is involved, you may have as little as six months to file a claim. Don't wait to find out.

faq.q: I wasn't in a crosswalk. Do I still have a case?
faq.a: Very likely. Drivers have a duty to watch for pedestrians everywhere, and California's comparative negligence rules mean you can recover even if you share some fault — your recovery is just reduced by your percentage. Don't let the insurer talk you out of a claim.

faq.q: It was a hit-and-run. Who pays?
faq.a: Possibly your own auto policy's uninsured-motorist coverage (even though you were on foot), a family member's policy, or — if the driver is later identified — theirs. We investigate every avenue.

faq.q: The driver's insurer already offered me money.
faq.a: Don't sign. Pedestrian injuries often get worse before they get better, and a signed release ends your claim permanently. A free review takes 60 seconds.

faq.q: How long do I have to file?
I don't have health insurance. Can I still get treated?
faq.a: Yes. We help clients get the care they need — often on a lien, so providers are paid from the settlement instead of out of your pocket. Don't skip treatment.
Nothing up front — ever. We front every cost of building your case and only collect a fee if we recover money for you. No recovery, no attorney fee.
